templates.name: Reactive Scene
templates.description: Inspired by Scene & Sequel and the Snowflake Method

children.text: A major plot twist appears. This keeps the story from just being on the same old, same old track.
This twist can put your character back to square one, rethink everything, even question her ability.

This is hard on your character and the reader, after all they're enjoying your book trying to figure who dunnit, and now your sleuth is really struggling. But you as the author must keep the story moving, the character must continue on despite the bad odds of getting whatever their goal is for the story to come to fruition. Justice, Vengeance,  Settling The Score, Acquittal, Trust etc.
This leads us to the Black Moment.
Scene One
Scene Two
Scene Three
Now that the sleuth has rebounded from the Black Moment and creates the climax, hoping it will work...
What kind of reveal do you want?
A room full of suspects that will act as the denouement?
Or a confrontation with the killer.
To know which is best, be sure you know your sleuth well enough to know they work better one way or the other. Or think they can which could then add complications.
Reveal more about your sleuth, history, conflicts, problems. (Make sure your GMC is built).
Remember your sleuth will move forward, then have to retrace their steps as their ideas DON'T pan out.
This long middle will also:
A. Reveal facts about suspects, through interrogations and the discovery of clues.
Bring more of your town in, repeating characters you're building for future books that perhaps been accused mistakenly and trust will need to be built again.  Or the opposite
B. Flight, or disappearance of one or more suspect.
C. Develop a sense of urgency. Raise the stakes or make it evident that if the mystery is not solved soon, there will be terrible consequences.
All of this leads to the midpoint.

cards.title: The sleuth takes on the case

children.text: By the end of ACT 1, the sleuth has to decide to take action. She/he cannot be still.
WHY, what's at stake for them if they do nothing?
And why does this person think they can do anything the police can't?
Set the scene, this is important in a cozy to ground the reader into the story.
Introduce Main Characters
Sleuth
The Formal Investigative Connection ie. Police
Sidekick of sleuth
The victim and why his/her death matters, how they were important to the town, good or bad.
various suspects or at least people who were in the prior introductions and chapters
Introduce the town,
Make a map
Find some interesting businesses that can move your story ahead,
Create characters for those businesses that are pro/con toward your sleuth.
Introduce the season
Remember to use that season in the book to add to the danger, the beauty, the sense of the town
The nuisance factor of the season
Layer in the attributes (see tab) for the characters introduced so far.
Usually by the END OF ACT ONE, you'll need your INCITING SCENE.
Usually the murder
The Black Moment
is often considered the false ending. It's the darkest moment in the book is when the protagonist (our sleuth) loses all hope.
Crisis: The worst has happened. Everything the characters have tried to avoid has come to fruition.
Usually revealed in a single scene, ending with things worse off than anyone realized.
But the story must continue, so the protagonist pulls themselves up,  and then the stakes are raised again as the book moves to its finale, the climax.
Climax:
The battle is being fought in an all-or-nothing struggle with the ending in still in doubt.
